git commit -q -F - <<'MSG' && git log --oneline -1
fix(connection): contain FSM failures, and say where and why a connect failed

Reliability, from testing against real hardware until the failure modes stopped
appearing:
  - IsolateTransport.request could hang forever. The timeout is enforced inside
    the isolate, so if it died, was killed mid-request, or a reply was lost, the
    completer never completed. Adds a deadline with slack, and dispose() now
    fails everything in flight instead of stranding callers (a service swap
    mid-request used to permanently wedge DeviceProvider.syncWithController,
    because its `finally` never ran).
  - One FSM attempt at a time: a caller arriving mid-attempt joins it, and this
    is the single place exceptions are contained. A throw from the ICE bridge or
    discovery used to escape through unawaited(connect()) and leave probing=true
    forever, so the UI sat on "Connecting..." until the app was killed.
  - Service swaps bump a generation and detach onReachability BEFORE dispose, so
    late timeouts from the old service can't repaint state for the new one.
  - A failing heartbeat now escalates to a real reconnect with backoff instead of
    re-probing a stale endpoint forever (after a DHCP change the app stayed
    offline on the same Wi-Fi until pull-to-refresh).
  - The ICE session is retained and its state watched after connect, and a
    localPort of 0 is treated as failure — that produced a "connected" hub that
    could never answer.
  - Observe subscriptions retry with backoff instead of dying silently.

Diagnostics: a failed connect reported "could not reach the controller", which is
true of every failure and useful for none. Each FSM stage is now named (network
check, LAN discovery, LAN probe, pairing lookup, rendezvous, ICE gather, ICE
connect, tunnel probe) and recorded per attempt with pass/fail/skipped, duration
and a detail line, surfaced as a LAST ATTEMPT card with copy-to-clipboard so a
failure can be reported from the phone that is failing — usually the off-LAN one,
nowhere near a machine with adb.

Making the "why" real needed the transport to stop discarding it:
TransportResponse gains an error, and the isolate boundary — which was literally
`onError: (_) => unreachable` — now carries the reason across. A DTLS rejection,
a timeout and an unreachable host used to be indistinguishable.

The remote path also now verifies the tunnel before reporting success (it was
fire-and-forget), so a tunnel that comes up but cannot carry CoAP fails at a
named stage instead of being unmasked later by a heartbeat.

test_live/ holds the hardware reliability tests; they sit outside test/ so CI
skips them, and read host/PSK from a local config so no secret is committed.

Built, analyzer clean, 98/98. No phone on the network to install to — give me a port when one's up.

**What "Future not completed" actually meant:** `awaitConnected` used a bare `.timeout(20s)`, and Dart's default `TimeoutException` message is that literal string. The real meaning: **ICE never reached `connected`, `failed` or `closed` within 20 seconds.** My diagnostics faithfully surfaced a message that says nothing — the exact failure mode the feature exists to prevent, so that's on me.

It now reports the last state actually observed, because the two plausible causes look identical otherwise:

- `ICE did not connect within 20 s (last state: checking)` → connectivity checks are running but no candidate pair succeeds. That's a real network problem — on 5G, likely the relay path.
- `ICE did not connect within 20 s (last state: none seen — no candidate pair succeeded, or the native state stream is silent)` → we never got *any* state callback, which points at the EventChannel rather than at ICE.
- `the ICE state stream closed before connecting (last state: …)` → the session died underneath us; previously this hung until the timeout instead of failing immediately.

The distinction matters: your earlier attempt got as far as **Tunnel probe**, which means `awaitConnected` *did* complete then — so the state stream works at least sometimes, and a "none seen" reading now would be a strong signal in its own right.

Once it's installed, the **Copy diagnostics** output will also show the `offer gathered: host=N srflx=N relay=N` and `answer received: …` counts plus every `ICE state:` transition, which together should say whether a relay candidate was present on both sides and how far the checks got.

One caveat worth stating: this is a diagnostics improvement, not a fix. If ICE genuinely can't connect on 5G, the next question is which candidate pair it's attempting — and that may want the STUN/TURN gather report we scoped earlier but haven't built.

**Your phone is now fully correct:** `ICE gather — host=2 srflx=2 relay=1`. It allocated a TURN relay, so the credentials and the whole app-side TURN path work.

The answer contained a `typ relay` candidate, which is what I verified, but the relay pair is only ever *selected* by a genuinely off-LAN peer. Your phone on 5G is the only thing that exercises it. I over-read "relay candidate present" as "relay path tested", and I should have been clearer that those aren't the same claim.

content.text:
Grounded answer: **rooms are purely app-local today.** `Room` + `MatterDevice.roomId`, persisted in SharedPreferences under `'rooms'` (`device_store.dart:15`), and the shared proto has **no room concept at all** — grep for room/label in `flux.proto` returns only an unrelated comment. The controller doesn't know rooms exist.

## Why that placement will hurt

You already have the cautionary tale in-tree: **energy roles are app-local and pushed one-way**, and nothing reads them back. The consequences are recorded pain — roles reset to `none` blank the house energy view, and they're wiped whenever a device is re-added. Rooms are the same shape of data and will reproduce it exactly:

- **Two phones disagree permanently.** You're running `.229` and A063 right now; rooms set on one are invisible on the other, forever.
- **Reinstall or clear-storage loses the whole layout** — the same class of loss as the phantom-controller episode earlier.
- **Re-adding a device drops it back to "No Room"**, because `roomId` lives on the app's device record and a re-add mints a fresh one.
- **The controller can't use rooms** for anything — no per-room energy attribution, no "run the dishwasher when the kitchen is cheap", no room-scoped automation. Given the energy-management pivot, that's the expensive one.

## Three candidate homes

**1. App-local (today).** Simple, works offline, no wire contract. But it's per-phone by construction, and rooms are a property of the *home*, not of a handset.

**2. Controller (recommended).** Same model as the device registry itself: controller is authoritative, app caches for offline display. Survives reinstalls, agrees across phones, and makes rooms available to controller-side logic.

**3. Matter User Label cluster (0x0041).** The spec's own answer for room assignment, fabric-scoped, and readable by Apple/Google — genuinely portable. But it can't hold Modbus/synthetic devices, it's an optional cluster, and it can't store the *room list* itself (an empty room would simply vanish). Good as a **mirror**, wrong as the store.

## The suggestion I'd actually make

Don't add a third per-device metadata mechanism. The controller already has **two** ad-hoc ones: `name` inside `flux_DeviceRecord`, and a separate `energy_roles` NVS blob that the app pushes one-way. Rooms would make three.

Fold them into **one controller-side per-device metadata record** — name, room, energy role — with the app as a cache rather than the owner. That single move kills the roles-wiped-on-re-add bug, the two-phones-disagree bug, and the rooms question together, and it gives the energy log a room dimension (the CSV already carries `DEVICE_NAME`; a room column is the natural companion).

Two design details worth deciding up front: membership stays device-side (`roomId` on the record, not a room→devices list) since that's already the shape and avoids two-way consistency; and the room list needs its own small store so empty rooms survive.

**One sequencing point:** this should come *after* the `dev_id` refactor (tasks #13–21), not before. Room membership has to key on something stable, and keying it on today's `node_id` would just have to be migrated again — plus "fresh identity per add" means a re-added device loses its room unless the metadata record is keyed on something that survives, which is exactly the trade-off you already chose there.

There's one honest counter-argument: `deviceNameForNode` carries a deliberate comment about resolving names locally "instead of trusting stale names baked into controller-side data", so someone chose local authority for names on purpose. That reasoning holds for *display during a stale connection* — which the cache covers — but not for ownership.

Two readings of that, and they lead to materially different refactors — worth pinning down before I start, since this is the foundation everything else keys on.

**Reading A — composite identity.** Drop the invented `dev_id` entirely; a device is identified on the wire by the **pair** `(kind, node_id)`. `node_id` keeps its meaning *within its namespace* (Matter operational node ID for Matter devices, a small counter for Modbus, an haId-derived id for cloud), and `kind` disambiguates. This is attractive: it removes the reserved `0x0100000000000000` range, removes the bit-63 rule, removes the need to mint a new identity at all — and it's literally "node_id and type as two selection criteria". Cost: every per-device message, cache and map key becomes two fields instead of one, including the fixed-size `notify_t` and the 32-entry attr caches in `flux_coap_notify.c` that currently compare a single `uint64`.

**Reading B — `dev_id` stays the key, `kind` and `node_id` become query criteria.** The registry keeps a single opaque identity as planned, and additionally exposes lookup/filter by kind and by node_id (`flux_device_by_kind()`, `flux_device_by_node()`), so the app can select "all Modbus devices" or resolve a Matter node without inference. Smaller change, single-field keys preserved.

I'd lean toward **A** if that's what you meant — it's less invented machinery than the approved plan, and it makes the type explicit rather than encoded, which was your original objection. The one thing I'd want to get right is representation: keeping `kind` as a separate field in the hot-path structs (explicit, +1 byte) rather than packing it into the top bits of the integer, since packing would quietly recreate the "type smuggled into a number" problem behind an accessor.

Kills the reserved synthetic range and the bit-63 contract outright, and nothing new is invented. Cost: two-field keys everywhere, including the fixed-size notify struct and the 32-entry attr caches that today compare one uint64.

options.label: B — dev_id key, kind+node_id as queries

feat(proto): identify devices by (kind, node_id) instead of a magic node range

A device is now identified by the PAIR (kind, node_id) — two selection criteria,
neither sufficient alone. node_id keeps its field number and its meaning, but
scoped to its kind's namespace: a real Matter operational node ID for MATTER, a
controller-assigned id for MODBUS and CLOUD.

This replaces inferring the kind from the magnitude of node_id. Synthetic devices
were handed Matter node IDs above a reserved base (0x0100000000000000) and every
consumer re-derived "is this really a Matter node?" from that constant. It was
duplicated across three repos, already stale and wrong in one of them, and it
forced a cross-repo rule that bit 63 stay clear because the app decodes node_id
into a signed integer. With kind carried explicitly the reserved range and the
bit-63 rule both disappear, and each namespace can number from 1.

kind is added as a new field on Device and on every per-device message
(AttrsUpdate, DeviceStateEvent, DeviceCommand, ReadRequest, WriteAttrRequest,
RenameDeviceRequest, EnergyRoleEntry, EnergyDeviceSeries). DEVICE_KIND_UNKNOWN=0
is deliberately not a synonym for Matter, so an unset field reads as a decode
error rather than silently meaning "Matter".

content.text:
**Foundation is in.** `(kind, node_id)` is now the wire identity, committed as `6272858` and pushed; both `flux-interface` checkouts are synced to it, and I verified a round-trip in C (nanopb regenerated), Dart (copied into `lib/services/proto/`, app analyzer clean) and Python (`node_id=42 kind=DEVICE_KIND_MODBUS`).

Design notes worth recording, since they shaped the edits:

- **`node_id` kept its field number and meaning**, just scoped per namespace. That makes this a much smaller change than the `dev_id` plan — no invented identity, no reserved range, and the bit-63 cross-repo rule is simply gone.
- **`DEVICE_KIND_UNKNOWN = 0` is deliberately not Matter.** With proto3 defaults, an unset field decodes as 0, so making UNKNOWN a synonym for Matter would silently mis-route anything that forgot to set it. It reads as a decode error instead.
- I routed the proto through **git rather than copying between checkouts** — my first attempt regenerated Python from `flux-controller/proto` and produced bindings with no `DeviceKind`, because the edit lived only in the app's working tree. Commit → push → `merge --ff-only` keeps one source of truth, which is the whole point given this repo's history of diverging.

Next up is the firmware registry (#14): `flux_dev_kind_t` in a neutral `devices/` header, `kind` on `flux_DeviceRecord`, lookups keyed on the pair, and deleting `FLUX_MODBUS_NODE_BASE` / `flux_is_modbus_node`.

One thing I want to flag before I go further, because it affects how much churn lands in one go: this is a **flag-day change** — once the firmware sends `kind`, an older app decodes it as `UNKNOWN`, and vice versa. So the firmware and app changes have to land together, and the controller can't be flashed independently of installing the app. I'll keep both sides building and only flash once both are ready, rather than leaving you with a half-migrated pair mid-session.

content.text:
Important — my justification was wrong, and the truth is worse. Measured:

- `dev_v0` = 88 bytes, `dev_v1` = **88 bytes** (identical), and `vendor_id` moved from offset 8 → 12. So an unmigrated record isn't *rejected*, it's **silently misread**: `kind` takes the low byte of `vendor_id` and every field after shifts.
- Same for roles: both 16 bytes, with `cls` at offset 8 being read as `kind`.
- Putting `kind` at the end doesn't help either — trailing padding absorbs it, still 88.

So the size check offers **zero** protection and the version key is the only guard. Let me correct the comments and drop the heuristic that pretended otherwise:

input.command:
cd /home/tado/workspace/flux/flux-controller && python3 - <<'PY'
p='firmware/main/matter/flux_state.c'
s=open(p).read()

# 1. the boot comment asserted the wrong failure mode
s = s.replace('''    /* Stamp `kind` onto records written before the field existed. Must run before
     * any reader: adding the field changed sizeof(flux_DeviceRecord), and every
     * load demands an exact size match, so without this every pre-existing
     * device and energy-role override silently disappears. */''',
'''    /* Stamp `kind` onto records written before the field existed. Must run before
     * any reader, and the exact-size check in dev_get_unlocked() does NOT protect
     * us: measured, v0 and v1 are both 88 bytes (the field fits in existing
     * padding), so an unmigrated record is not rejected — it is MISREAD, with
     * `kind` taking the low byte of vendor_id and every later field shifted.
     * The version key is therefore the only guard; see state_migrate_kind_v1. */''', 1)

# 2. drop the meaningless size heuristic (v0 and v1 roles are both 16 bytes)
s = s.replace('''    /* Already v1 if the size is a whole number of new records and not of old
     * ones; when both divide evenly the version key on the device namespace has
     * already been bumped, so this only runs once regardless. */
    if (sz % sizeof(role_record_v0_t) != 0) { nvs_close(h); return; }

    size_t n = sz / sizeof(role_record_v0_t);''',
'''    /* No size test is possible: role v0 and v1 are both 16 bytes (kind fits in
     * the padding after node_id), so v0 and v1 blobs are indistinguishable by
     * length. Correctness rests entirely on the version key checked by the
     * caller, which is why this must never be called directly. */
    if (sz % sizeof(role_record_v0_t) != 0) { nvs_close(h); return; }

    size_t n = sz / sizeof(role_record_v0_t);''', 1)

# 3. record the coincidence so nobody later assumes size separation exists
s = s.replace('''/* v0 layouts, frozen — never track changes to the live structs. */''',
'''/* v0 layouts, frozen — never track changes to the live structs.
 *
 * Both pairs are deliberately asserted to be the SAME size as their v1
 * counterparts. That is not a happy accident to rely on, it is a hazard to
 * remember: it means no reader can detect an unmigrated record by length, so the
 * version key is load-bearing. If a future field ever changes these sizes, the
 * asserts fire and this migration needs re-thinking rather than silent updating. */''', 1)

s = s.replace('''typedef struct {
    uint64_t node_id;
    uint8_t  cls;
} role_record_v0_t;''',
'''typedef struct {

_Static_assert(sizeof(role_record_v0_t) == sizeof(flux_EnergyRoleRec),

**Done and pushed:** the proto (`6272858`) — `(kind, node_id)` is the wire identity, verified round-tripping in C, Dart and Python, with both `flux-interface` checkouts synced via git rather than file copying.

**One thing worth reading closely, because I nearly shipped it on a false premise.** I wrote the migration justified by "adding the field changed the record size, so old records get rejected." Moving `kind` to the end doesn't help; trailing padding absorbs it.

'''/* Reject a node this file cannot act on. The old test was
 * flux_is_modbus_node(node_id) — "is this integer big enough to be synthetic?".
 * Now the registry answers directly, so a device of any future non-Matter kind is
 * rejected too rather than sneaking through on magnitude. */
static bool not_a_matter_node(uint64_t node_id)
{
    return flux_device_kind_of_node(node_id) != FLUX_DEV_KIND_MATTER;
}

/* ── Subscription attribute callbacks ────────────────────────────────────── */''', 1)

# every guard: same semantics, explicit source of truth
n_guards = s.count('flux_is_modbus_node(node_id)')
s = s.replace('flux_is_modbus_node(node_id)', 'not_a_matter_node(node_id)')

# metadata + emits are all MATTER here
s = s.replace('flux_device_set_metadata(node_id,', 'flux_device_set_metadata(FLUX_DEV_KIND_MATTER, node_id,')
s = s.replace('flux_events_emit_attr(node_id,', 'flux_events_emit_attr(FLUX_DEV_KIND_MATTER, node_id,')
s = s.replace('''                flux_events_emit_device(
                    n, (uint8_t)''', '''                flux_events_emit_device(

                        FLUX_DEV_KIND_MATTER, n, (uint8_t)''')

s = s.replace('flux_device_get_by_node(node_id, &rec)', 'flux_device_get_by(FLUX_DEV_KIND_MATTER, node_id, &rec)')
s = s.replace('flux_device_get_by_node(node_id, NULL)', 'flux_device_get_by(FLUX_DEV_KIND_MATTER, node_id, NULL)')

# FW-ADR-0009: Modbus devices are first-class devices under synthetic node IDs

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-07-30 (reconstructed from `matter/flux_state.h:145-166`)
- **Relates to:** flux-proto (the app decodes `node_id`; contract-adjacent)

## Context

flux manages Matter devices (real 64-bit operational node IDs, assigned from a
small counter starting at `0x0003`) and Modbus TCP/UDP devices (energy meters,
inverters). The app and the `/devices` API should treat both uniformly rather
than carry two parallel device concepts across the wire.

## Decision

Each Modbus device gets a **synthetic 64-bit node ID** `FLUX_MODBUS_NODE_BASE |
n` (`0x0100000000000000 | n`) and is mirrored into the same device registry as a
`flux_DeviceRecord`, so `/devices` lists Matter and Modbus devices
transparently. `flux_is_modbus_node(nid)` is the single discriminator. The base
is chosen to be **positive as a signed 64-bit integer** (bit 63 clear): the
phone app decodes `node_id` into a signed Dart int and formats it as hex for the
`?id=` query — a value with the top bit set would go negative and never match on
the controller (silent "no readings").

## Consequences

- One device model, one API surface, one identity type across Matter and Modbus
  — and across transports (the synthetic-ID scheme is transport-neutral).
- The bit-63-clear constraint is a **cross-repo contract** with the app: any
  future ID scheme (more synthetic ranges, other bus types) must keep IDs
  positive-signed or break the app's `?id=` round-trip silently. This is the
  kind of constraint that belongs in the shared proto ADR series too.
- The Modbus registry is separate config but every entry is mirrored into the
  Matter device table; the two must be kept consistent on upsert/remove.

## Alternatives considered

- **A separate Modbus API and device list** — duplicates enumeration, filtering,
  and naming; the app would carry two device concepts.
- **Use the full 64-bit space (bit 63 free)** — round-trips wrong through the
  app's signed-int decode; the exact silent-failure this base avoids.

# FW-ADR-0015: A device is identified by (kind, node_id)

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-08-10
- **Supersedes:** [FW-ADR-0009](0009-modbus-devices-as-synthetic-node-ids.md)
- **Relates to:** flux-proto (`DeviceKind`), flux-app, flux-ctl

## Context

ADR-0009 gave every Modbus device a **synthetic** 64-bit node ID
(`0x0100000000000000 | n`) so Matter and Modbus devices could share one registry
and one `/devices` API. The kind of a device was then recoverable only by testing
the *magnitude* of that integer — `flux_is_modbus_node(nid) ≡ nid >= BASE`.

That worked, and it cost more than it saved:

- The base constant was duplicated across three repos (firmware, app, flux-ctl,
  integration tests) and **two copies had already drifted** to a stale
  `0xFFFFFFFF00000000` from a superseded design.
- About ten independent guards each re-encoded "this integer is too large to be a
  Matter node, so I cannot talk to it" — a type question answered by arithmetic.
- It leaked a **cross-repo contract**: bit 63 had to stay clear purely because
  the app decodes `node_id` into a signed Dart int. Any future ID scheme
  inherited that constraint or broke the `?id=` round-trip silently.
- The energy CSV already recorded a `SOURCE` column (`matter | modbus`), so the
  on-disk log carried a kind the wire contract refused to.

A `node_id` is a Matter operational identifier allocated within a fabric. A
Modbus meter has no fabric, so naming it with one was a category error that a
third integration (Home Connect, whose native IDs are strings) would have made
worse.

## Decision

**Kind becomes explicit data, and identity becomes the pair `(kind, node_id)`.**

- A closed enum `DeviceKind { UNKNOWN=0, MATTER=1, MODBUS=2, CLOUD=3 }` lives in
  the shared proto and, as `flux_dev_kind_t`, in the neutral firmware header
  `main/devices/flux_device_kind.h` — deliberately not under `matter/`, so the
  taxonomy is not owned by one backend.
- `flux_DeviceRecord` gains a `kind` field. Every registry lookup takes the pair:
  `flux_device_get_by(kind, node_id)`, `flux_device_set_name(kind, node_id, …)`,
  `flux_energy_role_of(kind, node_id)`, and so on.
- `node_id` keeps its own meaning: the Matter operational node ID when
  `kind == MATTER`, and otherwise just the per-kind identifier the owning
  subsystem allocates. Modbus IDs now start at 1 from an ordinary counter.
- `FLUX_MODBUS_NODE_BASE` and `flux_is_modbus_node()` are **deleted**. The ten
  magnitude guards collapse into one registry question,
  `not_a_matter_node(node_id)` ⇒ `flux_device_kind_of_node(node_id) != MATTER`,
  so a device of any *future* non-Matter kind is rejected too instead of sneaking
  through because its ID happened to be small.
- `UNKNOWN = 0` is a decode error, never a synonym for MATTER. A peer that omits
  `kind` is handled by an explicit registry fallback (below), not by a default.

### Wire compatibility

`kind` is an **added** field, not a renumbering: `Device.kind = 8`, plus a `kind`
field on `AttrsUpdate`, `DeviceStateEvent`, `DeviceCommand`, `ReadRequest`,
`WriteAttrRequest`, `RenameDeviceRequest`, `EnergyRoleEntry` and
`EnergyDeviceSeries`. Per-device CoAP requests keep `?id=<hex>` and may add
`&kind=<n>`.

When a request arrives without `kind`, `resolve_kind_query()` looks the node ID
up in the registry and uses the kind it finds. This is unambiguous as long as one
node ID is not reused across kinds, which is true of all existing state — and it
is a lookup, never an inference from magnitude. New clients send `kind`
explicitly; all three (app, flux-ctl, integration tests) now do.

### Persisted-state migration

`flux_DeviceRecord` and `flux_EnergyRoleRec` are **the same size** before and
after (88 and 16 bytes; `_Static_assert`s pin this), because `kind` fell into
existing padding. Two consequences, both deliberate:

- An unmigrated record is **silently misread**, not rejected — the field offsets
  after `kind` shift. So migration must be unconditional, driven by an explicit
  `ver` key in the namespace, and cannot lean on a size heuristic.
- On upgrade, `kind` is reconstructed from the legacy encoding exactly once:
  `kind_from_legacy_node_id(nid) = nid >= 0x0100000000000000 ? MODBUS : MATTER`.
  This is the *only* place that constant survives, as a migration input.

## Consequences

- Routing by kind is a switch on data, so the eventual command bus resolves a
  backend from the record rather than from a bit test.
- The bit-63-clear cross-repo contract is gone, along with the encoding that
  needed it. IDs may use the full 64-bit space per kind.
- `kind` is mandatory in every new call path. The app's danger here is that
  Dart's `DeviceKind kind = DeviceKind.matter` default lets semantically wrong
  code compile silently — a missed `kind` on a device event stops Modbus
  readings reaching the UI without a single warning. The audited paths are
  `_toAppEvent`, `setEnergyRoles`, the `/events` observe, `DELETE /devices`, and
  `_subscribedNodeIds` (now keyed on the pair, since two kinds may share an ID).
- Adding a kind means: one proto enumerator, one `flux_dev_kind_t` value, one
  Dart enumerator — and no new identifier range to reserve.

## Alternatives considered

- **A controller-issued opaque `dev_id` replacing `node_id` on the wire** (the
  original plan). Cleaner in the abstract, but it renumbers most messages, breaks
  the energy-CSV join across the upgrade, forces an inbound
  `node_id → dev_id` map for CHIP callbacks (which only ever know a node ID), and
  needs its own counter and collision-avoidance rules. `(kind, node_id)` fixes
  the actual defect — kind inferred from magnitude — at a fraction of the blast
  radius, and leaves `dev_id` available if a kind ever needs a non-integer key.
- **A string identifier.** `notify_t` is a fixed-size struct in a 32-slot queue
  and the attribute caches are fixed arrays compared with `==`; strings would
  cost RAM per slot and turn every hot-path lookup into `strcmp`. A vendor's
  native string ID belongs in its own subsystem's table.
- **Keeping the synthetic ranges and adding `kind` as advisory metadata.** Leaves
  every magnitude guard in place and so leaves the bug class intact.

refactor(devices): identify a device by (kind, node_id)

Modbus devices used to live in a reserved node-id range
(0x0100000000000000 | n), so "what kind of device is this?" was answered by
testing the magnitude of an integer. That constant was duplicated across three
repos with two copies already drifted to a stale value, ~10 call sites each
re-encoded the same magnitude test, and it leaked a cross-repo contract: bit 63
had to stay clear purely because the app decodes node_id into a signed int.

Kind is now explicit data. flux_dev_kind_t lives in the neutral header
devices/flux_device_kind.h (not under matter/, so no backend owns the taxonomy),
DeviceKind rides the wire as an added field, and every registry lookup takes the
pair — flux_device_get_by(kind, node_id) and friends. FLUX_MODBUS_NODE_BASE and
flux_is_modbus_node() are gone; the magnitude guards collapse into one registry
question, which also rejects any future non-Matter kind instead of letting it
through on a small id.

Per-device CoAP requests may pass &kind=<n>; when it is absent the controller
resolves the kind from the registry rather than inferring it. flux-ctl and the
integration tests now send it explicitly.

Persisted state migrates in place, guarded by a version key rather than a size
check: measured, the v0 and v1 records are the SAME size (88 and 16 bytes — kind
fell into existing padding), so an unmigrated record is silently misread, not
rejected. _Static_asserts pin those sizes so a future field change fails the
build instead of the migration. The legacy base survives only as the migration's
input, mapping old ids to a kind exactly once.

_subscribedNodeIds is too, since two kinds may share a node id.

fabric can only ever address Matter devices, so only the controller port acts on
it and sends &kind= on /events and DELETE /devices.

content.text: Let me re-read the suggestion I gave you earlier so I build what we agreed, not something new:

result.output:
11 candidate messages
Grounded answer: **rooms are purely app-local today.** `Room` + `MatterDevice.roomId`, persisted in SharedPreferences under `'rooms'` (`device_store.dart:15`), and the shared proto has **no room concept at all** — grep for room/label in `flux.proto` returns only an unrelated comment. The controller doesn't know rooms exist.

## Why that placement will hurt

You already have the cautionary tale in-tree: **energy roles are app-local and pushed one-way**, and nothing reads them back. The consequences are recorded pain — roles reset to `none` blank the house energy view, and they're wiped whenever a device is re-added. Rooms are the same shape of data and will reproduce it exactly:

- **Two phones disagree permanently.** You're running `.229` and A063 right now; rooms set on one are invisible on the other, forever.
- **Reinstall or clear-storage loses the whole layout** — the same class of loss as the phantom-controller episode earlier.
- **Re-adding a device drops it back to "No Room"**, because `roomId` lives on the app's device record and a re-add mints a fresh one.
- **The controller can't use rooms** for anything — no per-room energy attribution, no "run the dishwasher when the kitchen is cheap", no room-scoped automation. Given the energy-management pivot, that's the expensive one.

## Three candidate homes

**1. App-local (today).** Simple, works offline, no wire contract. But it's per-phone by construction, and rooms are a property of the *home*, not of a handset.

**2. Controller (recommended).** Same model as the device registry itself: controller is authoritative, app caches for offline display. Survives reinstalls, agrees across phones, and makes rooms available to controller-side logic.

**3. Matter User Label cluster (0x0041).** The spec's own answer for room assignment, fabric-scoped, and readable by Apple/Google — genuinely portable. But it can't hold Modbus/synthetic devices, it's an optional cluster, and it can't store the *room list* itself (an empty room would simply vanish). Good as a **mirror**, wrong as the store.

## The suggestion I'd actually make

Don't add a third per-device metadata mechanism. The controller already has **two** ad-hoc ones: `name` inside `flux_DeviceRecord`, and a separate `energy_roles` NVS blob that the app pushes one-way. Rooms would make three.

Fold them into **one controller-side per-device metadata record** — name, room, energy role — with the app as a cache rather than the owner. That single move kills the roles-wiped-on-re-add bug, the two-phones-disagree bug, and the rooms question together, and it gives the energy log a room dimension (the CSV already carries `DEVICE_NAME`; a room column is the natural companion).

Two design details worth deciding up front: membership stays device-side (`roomId` on the record, not a room→devices list) since that's already the shape and avoids two-way consistency; and the room list needs its own small store so empty rooms survive.

**One sequencing point:** this should come *after* the `dev_id` refactor (tasks #13–21), not before. Room membership has to key on something stable, and keying it on today's `node_id` would just have to be migrated again — plus "fresh identity per add" means a re-added device loses its room unless the metadata record is keyed on something that survives, which is exactly the trade-off you already chose there.

There's one honest counter-argument: `deviceNameForNode` carries a deliberate comment about resolving names locally "instead of trusting stale names baked into controller-side data", so someone chose local authority for names on purpose. That reasoning holds for *display during a stale connection* — which the cache covers — but not for ownership.

Want me to write this up as an ADR with the proto sketch and migration path, or leave it as a note until the `dev_id` work lands?

feat(proto): rooms and per-device metadata owned by the controller

Rooms were phone-local (SharedPreferences), so two phones disagreed forever, a
reinstall lost the whole layout, and re-adding a device silently dropped it back
to "No Room" — the same failure the app-local energy roles already had. Both now
live on the device record the controller owns, with the app as a cache.

Room ids are small controller-issued integers rather than the app's UUIDs:
Device.room_id sits in a fixed-size NVS record where 2 bytes beats 37. Id 0 is
the "No Room" sentinel and is never stored or listed. Membership stays on the
device, not as a room→devices list, so there is only one copy of the
relationship.

DeviceMeta uses `optional` on every writable field: clearing a room and clearing
an energy role are legitimate writes, and without presence they are
indistinguishable from an untouched field.

EnergyRoleEntry/EnergyRoleMap are removed rather than deprecated. The role is
now Device.energy_class, written through the same DeviceMeta path — leaving a
second way to set one field is how the app's copy and the controller's drifted
apart to begin with. The app is not released, so there is nothing to keep
compatible.

input.command:
cd /home/tado/workspace/flux/flux-controller && git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'MSG' && git log --oneline -1
feat(rooms): the controller owns rooms and per-device metadata

Rooms lived only in the phone's SharedPreferences, so two phones disagreed
permanently, a reinstall lost the layout, and re-adding a device dropped it back
to "No Room". Energy roles had the same shape and the same bugs, plus a second
storage mechanism: an NVS blob the app pushed one-way that nothing read back.

Both now live on the device record — room_id and energy_cls beside name — so
there is ONE per-device metadata record and the controller owns it. Rooms are a
small NVS table (id, name) with a monotonic id counter. Ids are never reused: a
device still pointing at a deleted room would otherwise be silently adopted by
whichever room inherited the number, which is a wrong answer that looks valid.
Instead the reference matches nothing and is reset to No Room, logged.

flux_energy_roles_set and the roles blob are gone; flux_energy_role_of now reads
the device record, so the energy log is unchanged. GET/PUT /rooms replaces the
list wholesale (PUT answers with the assigned ids, which the caller has no other
way to learn) and POST /devices/meta does partial updates — every writable field
is `optional` on the wire because 0 is meaningful for both room (No Room) and
energy class (no override), so "absent" must stay distinct from "zero".

The migration chain is now v0 -> v1 -> v2, each step converting between frozen
copies of the layouts rather than the live struct. v2 records are 96 bytes where
v1 was 88, so unlike the v0/v1 step a stale record now fails the exact-size check
and disappears loudly instead of being misread — a _Static_assert fails the build
if a future edit makes those sizes match again.

Verified on hardware: 10/10 devices survive, rooms and assignments persist across
a reboot, deleting a room resets exactly the affected device, a re-created room
gets a fresh id, and energy class survives a room change.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

content.text: The fold as built would have been lossy: `carCharger` and `heatPump` both collapse to class 3, so the app would still need its own copy of the user's choice — the exact drift we're removing. Correcting it to store the *role* and derive the log class:

input.command:
cd /home/tado/workspace/flux/flux-app && cp flux-interface/generated/dart/flux.pb*.dart lib/services/proto/ && cd flux-interface && git add -A && git commit -q -m "$(cat <<'MSG'
feat(proto): store the energy ROLE, not just the derived class

Device.energy_class held the coarse log class (grid/pv/load/battery), but the
user assigns something finer: a car charger and a heat pump are both `load` to
the energy log and are not remotely the same thing to the person assigning them.
Storing only the class would have left the app keeping its own copy of the
distinction — the exact split that let rooms and roles drift apart.

Device.energy_role carries the assignment; the controller derives EnergyClass
from it when classifying a reading, so the energy log and history are unchanged.
ENERGY_ROLE_LOAD exists for one reason: a pre-rooms override was persisted as a
class, so a legacy `load` cannot say which kind of consumer it was. It is where
those land until the phone re-uploads the real answer, and it is not offered in
the picker.

The device record held the derived log class, which cannot represent what the
user actually assigned: a car charger and a heat pump are both `load`. Storing
only the class would have left the app keeping a private copy of the

the phone uploads the real assignment.

flux-ctl gains `rooms ls/add/rm/assign` and `role`, and the devices table gains

input.command:
git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'MSG' && git log --oneline -1
feat(rooms): the controller owns rooms and energy roles; app caches them

Rooms lived in this phone's SharedPreferences with UUID ids, so two phones
disagreed permanently, a reinstall lost the layout, and re-adding a device
dropped it back to "No Room". Energy roles had the same shape and the same bugs.
Both are now read from the controller and written through it.

Room.id becomes a controller-issued int, and createRoom returns null when the
controller is unreachable rather than minting a local id — a phone-side id is
precisely the divergence this replaces, so the UI says the room was not created
instead of showing one that would vanish on the next sync.

The hand-off is one-shot and recorded: on the first sync, this phone's rooms are
re-created on the controller, its per-device assignments remapped from UUID to
the issued ids, and its energy roles pushed. It runs BEFORE reconcile, because
reconcile treats the controller as authoritative for room and role — and on that
first sync the controller has neither, so the other order would wipe the layout
a moment before uploading it. Reconcile's adoption stays suppressed until the
flag is set, so a failed upload leaves the local copy intact to retry.

Two things that would have bitten quietly:
- Room.fromJson now parses `id` as int, and a legacy UUID makes `as int` throw a
  TypeError — an Error, not an Exception, which the store's `on Exception` would
  have let escape and take the whole room load with it.
- The legacy UUIDs cannot be read back through Room or MatterDevice at all, so
  the store gained raw readers for them; without those the hand-off would have
  had nothing to map.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

name: energy-roles-app-local-only
description: Live energy house view blanks because energy roles are app-local only and reset to none on controller device re-add
metadata:

Energy roles (EnergyRole on MatterDevice) are stored **only** in the app's local
state and pushed **one-way** to the controller via `POST /energy/roles` (which the
controller uses solely to classify its energy-history log). The `Device` message from
`GET /devices` carries **no** role field, and there is no `GET /energy/roles` — so the
app can never restore roles from the controller.

The live house view (`house_energy_scene.dart` → `DeviceProvider.energySummary` →
`EnergySummary.fromDevices`) reads ONLY local `energyRole`; a device with
`energyRole == none` contributes no node, so if all roles are `none` the scene shows
just the "HOME 0.00 W" pill even while the hub is online and live power flows.

Roles get wiped whenever `_reconcileWithController` (device_provider.dart ~414-465)
(re)creates a controller device — it builds them with `energyRole: none` and its
stale-purge removes+re-adds any device the controller momentarily stops reporting
(e.g. Modbus synthetic node churn). Diagnosed 2026-07-16: blank live view, hub Local,
SunSpec 103 producing 90 W, history correct, but device settings showed
"Not in energy overview".

**Why:** the controller is the real cross-device source of truth for classification
but the app treats local state as authoritative and can't read roles back.
**How to apply:** immediate recovery = re-assign roles per device in settings. Durable
fix = either preserve roles across purge/re-add app-side, or add role to the Device
proto / a `GET /energy/roles` (needs controller firmware). See [[flux-energy-management]],
[[flux-proto-dart-bindings]].

---
name: energy-roles-app-local-only
description: FIXED 2026-08-11 — rooms and energy roles now live on the controller's device record; app is a cache
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 336b3813-63b0-431c-b3d7-c5d1e1a6f5b8
---

**Resolved 2026-08-11.** Rooms and energy roles are now controller-owned, on the
device record (`flux_DeviceRecord.room_id` / `.energy_role`), and the app caches
them. `Device` carries `room_id` and `energy_role`; writes go through
`POST /devices/meta` (partial update — every writable field is `optional`,
because 0 is meaningful for both "No Room" and "no role"). Rooms are a separate
controller table behind `GET/PUT /rooms`, with controller-issued int ids that are
never reused. `POST /energy/roles`, `EnergyRoleMap` and the `energy_roles` NVS
blob are all gone.

The record stores the **role**, not the derived log class: a car charger and a
heat pump are both `load` to the energy log, so storing only the class would
force the app to keep a private copy of the distinction — which is exactly what
caused the original drift. `class_from_role()` in `flux_state.c` is the one place
the derivation happens.

**The original bug (for context):** roles lived only in app state and were pushed
one-way, so the live house view blanked whenever `_reconcileWithController`
re-created a controller device with `energyRole: none`, and two phones could
never agree. Rooms had the identical shape and the identical bug.

**Why it matters now:** the app must never write a room id it invented —
`createRoom` returns null when the controller is unreachable rather than minting
one locally. And on first sync a phone hands its old layout over
(`_uploadLocalLayoutOnce`) **before** reconcile, because reconcile treats the
controller as authoritative and would otherwise wipe the layout a moment before
uploading it.

**How to apply:** if roles or rooms look wrong, check the controller first
(`flux-ctl devices` shows Room and Role columns; `flux-ctl rooms ls`), not the
phone. See [[flux-energy-management]], [[flux-proto-dart-bindings]].

content.text:
Rooms now live on the controller. What shipped:

**Design** — one per-device metadata record (`name`, `room_id`, `energy_role`) that the controller owns and the app caches, plus a controller-owned room table so empty rooms survive. Room ids are controller-issued `uint16` and **never reused**, so a device pointing at a deleted room can't be silently adopted by a new one — it resolves to nothing and falls back to No Room, logged.

**One correction I made mid-build, worth knowing about:** I first stored the derived energy *class*. That's lossy — `carCharger` and `heatPump` both collapse to `load`, so the app would still have needed its private copy of the user's choice, which is the exact drift we were removing. The record now stores the **role**, and `class_from_role()` derives the log class in one place, so the energy log is unchanged.

**Verified on hardware** (controller + flux-ctl): rooms create/list/delete, assignment, roles, all surviving a reboot; deleting "Roof" reset exactly the one device that pointed at it; the re-created room got id 4, not 3.

Two things you should know:

1. **I can't confirm the old energy-roles blob carried anything into the records.** After the fold, every device read `UNKNOWN`. That's consistent with the blob having been empty, but I can't prove it: I erased the source without dumping it first, and the boot log that would have said `N role(s) folded in` was missed both times because the serial logger attaches ~30 s after reset. The practical impact is limited — classification falls back to the profile heuristic (grid meter still classifies as grid, inverter as pv), and the phone re-uploads its own roles on first sync. But it's an unverified step, not a verified one.

2. **The app leg is untested on device** — no phone is attached. `flutter analyze` is clean and all 98 tests pass, and the APK is built at `build/app/outputs/flutter-apk/app-debug.apk`. Give me a port and I'll install it and check the one path that matters most: the first sync handing your existing rooms and roles to the controller before reconcile can overwrite them.

One loose end I'd rather flag than bury: the intermediate firmware I flashed for ~15 minutes wrote *class* values into the same byte that now holds *role*. For grid (1) and pv (2) the numbers coincide, which is why your bench state is correct — but a 3 or 4 written by that build would now read as car-charger/heat-pump. I re-set both roles explicitly via flux-ctl, so this device is clean; no released build was ever affected.

Pushed: `b397808` (controller), `da2dc27` (app), `3123b18` (proto). Task #22 — narrowing the Matter subscription attribute paths — is still open.

feat(devices): sync device names with the controller

Name sat in the same controller-owned metadata record as room and energy role,
but the app still treated it as local-only: a rename never left the phone, and
reconcile never adopted the controller's. So names were the last piece that
disagreed between phones.

Renames now write through, and reconcile adopts the controller's name — but only
a non-empty one, since an empty name means the controller never learned it and
adopting that would blank a good local name.

The ordering matters more here than it did for rooms. The controller's name for a
Matter device comes from Basic Info at commissioning — "IKEA of Sweden", "Test
Vendor 1" — so adopting before handing the local names over would replace the
user's own names with vendor strings. Hence a one-shot upload that runs first,
pushing only names that actually differ.

That upload has its OWN flag rather than reusing layoutUploaded: phones that
already ran the rooms/roles hand-off must still upload their names, and sharing
the flag would skip exactly those phones — silently overwriting the user's names
on the next sync. This phone was one of them.

deviceNameForNode now takes the kind too; a node id alone does not identify a
device, and the PV series it serves is usually Modbus.

3	description: Flux app UI design system — Teenage-Engineering-inspired conventions for building/settings screens (tokens, panels, wording, connection state)
4	---
5	
6	# Flux UI — design system
7	
8	The concrete design language for the Flux Flutter app, distilled from the
9	Teenage Engineering sensibility: **form follows function, ruthless clarity,
10	technical-but-friendly, restraint over decoration.** Use this when building or
11	reworking any settings/config surface so screens stay consistent.
12	
13	For open-ended critique of an existing screen, use the `design-review` skill
14	(the TE persona). This skill is the rulebook — the tokens and patterns already
15	agreed on.
16	
17	## First principles
18	
19	1. **Two devices, always distinguishable.** The system is a **controller** (the
20	   Flux hardware) and **this phone**. Every screen must make clear which box a
21	   setting acts on. The top-level model is two labelled panels: `CONTROLLER`
22	   and `THIS PHONE`.
23	2. **One word: "controller."** Never "hub" in user-facing copy (buttons,
24	   titles, snackbars, logs the user reads, status). Code identifiers
25	   (`HubConnection`, `ControllerStatus.noHub`) are exempt — internal only.
26	3. **Say the state in plain language.** "Connected", "Offline", "Connecting…"
27	   — not jargon. Keep protocol nouns (fabric, dataset, Ext PAN ID) *inside*
28	   detail screens, never on menu tiles.
29	4. **Icons earn their place.** No decorative leading icons on nav rows. The
30	   only iconography that survives is meaningful: the connection-state **dot**
31	   and the trailing chevron. When in doubt, remove it.
32	
33	## Tokens
34	
35	Connection-state accents (define as file-level consts; keep identical across
36	screens):
37	
38	```dart
39	const _onlineColor     = Color(0xFF9FD8A8); // green  — connected, local
40	const _remoteColor     = Color(0xFFA9C7F2); // blue   — connected, remote tunnel
41	const _connectingColor = Color(0xFFBFC4CC); // grey   — connecting / standby / off
42	const _offlineColor    = Color(0xFFF2A9A0); // coral  — offline / error
43	```
44	
45	**Panel label** (the TE instrument-panel header) — wide-tracked monospace,
46	uppercase, muted, no glyph:
47	
48	```dart
49	Text(text, style: TextStyle(
50	  fontFamily: 'monospace', fontSize: 12, fontWeight: FontWeight.w700,
51	  letterSpacing: 2.4, color: cs.onSurfaceVariant));
52	// padding: EdgeInsets.fromLTRB(20, 0, 20, 10)
53	```
54	
55	**Grouping** — one `Card` per panel (`margin: horizontal 16`,
56	`clipBehavior: Clip.antiAlias`), rows separated by
57	`Divider(height: 1, indent: 16, endIndent: 16, color: cs.outlineVariant)`.
58	
59	**Nav row** — `ListTile(title: Text(label), trailing: Icon(chevron_right))`.
60	No leading icon.
61	
62	## Patterns
63	
64	**Connection widget.** The `CONTROLLER` panel opens with a dedicated
65	connection-state tile: coloured dot (leading) + plain state ("Connected") +
66	one-line detail ("Local network" / "Remote · encrypted tunnel"), tapping
67	through to a Connection detail screen. State → (dot, title, subtitle) via a
68	`switch` on `ControllerStatus` + `ConnectionKind`.
69	
70	**Connection detail screen.** Breaks the single live connection into its two
71	independent paths — `LOCAL NETWORK` and `REMOTE ACCESS` — each a card with a
72	State row (label left, dot + value right) and value rows (monospace, right-
73	aligned, ellipsised). `ConnectionKind` is mutually exclusive (loopback host =
74	remote, else local), so the inactive path reads "Standby".
75	
76	**Scope-split screens.** When a concept exists on both devices (Matter,
77	Thread), don't cram both into one screen with sections — parameterise the
78	screen with a scope enum (`MatterScope { controller, phone }`,
79	`ThreadScope { controller, phone }`) and route two separate menu entries, one
80	under each panel. Controller scope shows the real fabric / operational Thread
81	network + Sync; phone scope shows this phone's admin identity / scanned
82	credentials. Keep the appBar title plain ("Matter", "Thread"); the panel the
83	user came from plus the in-screen caption carry the "whose" context.
84	
85	## Reference implementation
86	
87	- `lib/ui/screens/settings_screen.dart` — the two-panel layout + tokens.
88	- `lib/ui/screens/settings/connection_screen.dart` — local/remote detail.
89	- `lib/ui/screens/settings/matter_settings_screen.dart` / `thread_settings_screen.dart`
90	  — the scope-split pattern.

content.text:
Installed on your phone. **Settings → CONTROLLER → Rooms**.

```
Rooms
┌──────────────────────────────────┐
│ Living Room                    ✕ │
│ No devices                       │
├──────────────────────────────────┤
│ Basement                       ✕ │
│ 5 devices                        │
└──────────────────────────────────┘
```

Three judgment calls worth naming:

**Under CONTROLLER, not a phone section.** Rooms live on the controller now, so the screen is a view of its list. Putting it anywhere else would imply this phone owns them.

**Only removal.** Creating stays in the picker, at the moment you actually want a room — while assigning a device. This screen does the one thing those flows can't express, so it stays a list and an ✕ rather than becoming a second place to manage rooms.

**The confirmation names the consequence.** "5 devices will move to No Room. Nothing is removed from your home." Deleting a room never deletes a device — the controller resets each one — and you shouldn't have to learn that by trying it. If the controller doesn't accept the delete, the row stays put rather than vanishing and reappearing on the next sync.

I followed the `flux-ui` rulebook I found in the repo: panel card, hairline dividers, no decorative leading icons.

An empty-but-non-null device list was treated as authoritative, so a single odd
answer purged every controller-managed device. They return on the next sync, but

content.text:
Investigated. **I could not reproduce the empty/sonar state** — right now the app is `Local`, 10 devices, 9 of them carrying fresh live readings (Grid Meter 658 W, SMGW 664 W, Eve on, tado setpoints). Only LEDVANCE has none, and it's offline. But the hunt found three real defects, all now fixed and deployed:

**1. `/events` never sent the device kind** — the actual bug. `hnd_events_get` set `node_id` but not `kind`, so every notification decoded as `unknown`, matched no device in the app, and was **dropped**. Values still refreshed on explicit reads, which is precisely what hid it: transport healthy, attributes present, only the live push dead. This is the exact failure mode the `(kind, node_id)` work warned about — a field defaulting to a plausible zero on a path with no error to raise — and the events handler was the one place I missed it.

**2. One empty device list could wipe your home.** An empty-but-non-null list was treated as authoritative, so a single odd answer purged every controller device. They come back next sync — but as *new* records with new ids, orphaning the live cache keyed by id, so **every card goes blank**. That is a very good match for what you saw, and my repeated flashes are exactly when a controller would be up but not yet answering normally. Now two consecutive empty answers are required, and the first one logs.

**3. The purge matched on `nodeId` alone**, not the full key. Same class as #1; now consistent.

Two things I should be straight about:

- **The empty cards you're seeing are not a bug.** `DeviceCard` renders only a name and product string over a `Spacer()` — no icon, no reading, no toggle. It's been byte-identical since April (`32c35c2`), so nothing I changed caused it. If you expected readings on the tiles, that's a feature that was never wired up, and I'd be glad to add it.
- I twice concluded things from missing log lines that turned out to be wrong — "no `/events` requests" (the controller just doesn't log them) and a mis-parsed snapshot blob. The controller's power-cycle at 09:36 was `rst:0x1 (POWERON)`, not a crash; heap was healthy right before.

To pin down what you actually saw, which was it: **"NO DEVICES"**, **"CONTROLLER OFFLINE"**, or a category screen like **"NO LIGHTING"**? Each has a different cause, and the wording tells me which. If it was the first two, fix #2 above most likely already covers it.

Pushed: `0ab9c52` (firmware, flashed), `9a1a760` (app, installed).

content.text:
Installed on the **Pixel 6** — and it just produced the proof the whole rooms/names move was for.

The Pixel already holds the controller's state: rooms `5 Basement` / `6 Home Office` with the *controller's* ids, the same per-device room assignments, and the same names. Two phones agreeing on a home layout is exactly what wasn't possible before today.

It also shows you've been using it: the controller now has **11** devices — `0x2B Watertap` is new — and `0x27` has been renamed `Ecklampe`. That rename came from a phone, went to the controller, and is what `flux-ctl` reads back. Round-trip confirmed on real use rather than on my test data.

One thing I checked before you opened it, and want to flag as a genuine edge I left in:

**A stale phone can still overwrite good names.** The one-time name hand-off pushes any local name that differs from the controller's — so a phone that had been sitting untouched for weeks would, on its first sync, push its old names over newer ones from another phone. It was harmless here (the Pixel's names already matched, and only `0x17`/`0x27` were user-edited), but the logic doesn't actually check *who edited more recently* — the controller stores no timestamp for it. Rooms don't have this problem: that upload is skipped entirely once the controller has any.

The fix I'd suggest is to push only names the user actually edited on that phone (`lastModified > commissionedAt` marks those, and I can see it in the stored records — the Pixel has exactly two). That would have handed over `Ikea Plug` and `Ecklampe` and left the vendor defaults alone. Small change; say the word and I'll make it.

Also: the Nothing phone at `.179` has dropped its wireless-debugging port again, so the scrcpy mirror is gone with it. The Pixel is connected now if you'd rather mirror that one.

Base directory for this skill: /tmp/claude-1001/bundled-skills/2.1.235/76956e01bd77139b8d42088f7f6e5ff2/artifact-capabilities

# Artifact runtime capabilities

A published Artifact page can declare **runtime capabilities** — abilities the claude.ai viewer grants the page at open time — by passing `capabilities: {name: config}` to the Artifact tool. The control plane is the authority on valid names and config shapes. Declaration gestures: **omitting** `capabilities` on a redeploy carries the stored declaration forward unchanged (and preserves the artifact's stored contract pin); an **empty object** `{}` is the explicit clear-all; a **non-empty object** is a full-set declaration (anything stored but not restated is revoked). Moving a republished artifact's runtime version is a deliberate gesture — pass `contract: 'latest'` to upgrade, or a specific version to pin or roll back — never a side effect of editing.

**Available capabilities:** `artifact`, `downloads`, `mcp`, `self` — the complete set of capability names you may declare. Anything not listed is unavailable to this user.

Runtime contract 0.2.9


Capability namespaces live behind `claude.use(name)`: `const db = await claude.use("db")` resolves the capability's namespace once this view can run its code, or `null` when it cannot — not served here, not granted at initialization, or failed to load, indistinguishable by design. Branch on `null` and design for absence; never probe `window.claude` members. Permission stays on the calls themselves: a consent prompt, rate limit, or policy refusal arrives on the first call, never from `use()`. For capabilities this view serves, the promise is memoized — awaiting `use("db")` again is free; an unknown name resolves `null`. Works for every capability this contract serves; each capability's own section and type definitions document its namespace.


--- capability: artifact ---

Use `artifact` for pages that should remember what people do with them: polls, sign-up sheets, checklists, trackers, boards — the page is the record. Declare `capabilities: {artifact: {}}`; owner and editors write as themselves; read-only viewers reject `not_granted`/`not_writer` — show a read-only view. On a LIVE DOC the page's markup IS the shared document: whatever a viewer's click or keystroke changes in the DOM (text, attributes, elements, checkbox/input state) is saved as them and reaches every view and Claude; what script does with no gesture (load, timers, fetch) is not. Write content as HTML in the page and mutate it directly in handlers, never render it from a JS object, and keep per-viewer UI (filters, tabs, sort order, drafts) inside `<artifact-local>` or on `data-local-*` attributes. On a classic artifact `const artifact = await claude.use("artifact")`, then `artifact.publish(html)` saves a new version; `conflict` is routine: keep the source a render function of state, never the live DOM.


--- capability: downloads ---

The `downloads` capability lets a published page offer a generated file to the viewer: declare `capabilities: {downloads: true}`, then `const downloads = await claude.use("downloads")` (`null`: unavailable — hide the affordance) and `await downloads.save({filename, data})`. The viewer sees a confirmation and may decline — a save is never silent or guaranteed, so offer it on explicit viewer intent and handle rejection. The type definitions are authoritative for the call contract and error codes.


--- capability: mcp ---

`mcp` lets a published page call the viewer's claude.ai connectors: `const mcp = await claude.use("mcp")` (`null`: unavailable); calls run with the viewer's credentials, never exposing tokens. Declare `capabilities: {mcp: {servers: [{server, tools}]}}` — `server` is a connector's display name. Keep the manifest minimal: it is a viewer-consented grant; a declaring page cannot be shared publicly. Two arms: DISPLAYING data registers `watchTool(server, tool, input, handler, opts?)` — replays cache, refreshes when stale, polls only via `refetchInterval`, returns a sync unsubscribe; an ACTION calls `callTool` once and reads `result.payload`. Tool failures REJECT (`tool_error`); watch failures arrive as handler error events. Type definitions first: branch UX per error code, retry only `retryable` errors, drop data on authz denials, drive freshness UI from `result.cache.storedAt`. They omit argument names and result encoding: observe a real request/response pair per tool, or say so at publish — never guess.


--- capability: self ---

`self` is the former name of the `artifact` capability (renamed). It remains for compatibility: published pages and previously generated code that declare `capabilities: {self: {}}`, feature-check `window.claude.self`, or call `claude.use("self")` keep working unchanged — both names resolve this same capability. Do not use it in new pages: declare `capabilities: {artifact: {}}` and obtain the namespace with `await claude.use("artifact")`; see the artifact section for how to use it.


**Your connectors this session.** None are connected right now — they may still be connecting, or the user has none. Look for tools prefixed `mcp__claude_ai_*` in your tool list; each is named `mcp__claude_ai_<connector>__<tool>`. Only claude.ai connectors are valid — locally-configured MCP servers are not. The manifest's `tools` array takes the connector's upstream tool names (as returned by `listTools()` / `/v1/mcp_servers`), which can differ from the normalized `<toolName>` segment when an upstream name contains `.` or spaces. In hermetic/CI sessions where connectors aren't loaded but `$CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` is set, fetch the list via Bash: `curl -H 'anthropic-version: 2023-06-01' -H 'anthropic-beta: mcp-servers-2025-12-04' -H "Authorization: Bearer $CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN" https://api.anthropic.com/v1/mcp_servers?limit=1000`; in that case use each entry's `display_name` as the `server` value (exact display names are always accepted alongside tool-prefix segments).

content.text:
**https://claude.ai/code/artifact/3d3b83b5-1dc5-47c0-93cc-863312ab7358**

Three directions, all built on your existing tokens — the scene's pastel accents, 22px radii, monospace panel labels. Each has a **Solar surplus / Evening draw** toggle so you can see the flow reverse, which is the thing a static mockup can't tell you.

**A · Flow hub** — the familiar solar-app metaphor. Solar above, home below, grid and battery either side; position carries the meaning. Direction is the *animation* (dashes drift source→target), not an arrowhead, so it reads at a glance without decoration. Best instant read of what's feeding what; costs the most vertical space and says little about proportion.

**B · Balance bar** — everything coming in on top, everything going out below, ribbons showing which source pays for which use, widths to scale. It's a Sankey small enough to compute in ~15 lines. Best at proportion: you *see* solar covering the house and the surplus splitting. Needs a beat of learning.

**C · Flow ledger** — one row per real transfer, nothing drawn for a path carrying nothing. The most Teenage Engineering of the three: instrument readout, no picture. Most precise, smallest, and scales to a car charger or heat pump for free — but you read it rather than glance at it.

On **state of charge**: it appears in all three, but I treated it as a *state, not a flow* — B and C give it its own ten-cell gauge on its own row, so it stays visible when the battery is idle and no flow line is drawn. A tucks a hairline under the battery node, which is tighter but disappears into the diagram.

Two things from the code while I was in there:

- **`batterySocPercent` already exists** in `EnergySummary` and is populated from `batteryPercent` — averaged across battery devices. Nothing renders it. So the app side may need less than you think; it depends what your controller work exposes.
- **I fixed a bug I introduced earlier today.** In `EnergySummary.fromDevices`, stacked `case` labels share a body in Dart, so `case EnergyRole.load:` sitting above `case EnergyRole.grid:` was silently summing generic consumers into **grid import**. A `load` device now contributes no node — its draw is already in the balance and lands in `restOfHome`.

My recommendation: **C for the home screen strip, A for the Energy tab.** The ledger earns the always-visible slot because it's honest at small size and never draws a path that isn't carrying anything; the hub earns the tab because that's where you go to actually understand the house. Tell me which way you'd go and I'll build it against the real summary.

Three versions of C, now with the car, wallbox and heat pump in the mix.

**Open locally** (no login needed): `file:///home/tado/workspace/flux/flux-app/.design/energy/preview.html` — I've opened it on your desktop. Same thing on the canvas: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/3d3b83b5-1dc5-47c0-93cc-863312ab7358

All three run the same underlying allocation — a greedy attribution of each source to each use — and differ in what a *row* is about. Toggle **Solar surplus / Evening draw**; the evening case is where they separate.

**C1 · Attribution** — one row per transfer: `SOLAR → CAR 3.6 kW`. Reads as sentences. Strongest when you want to know *where the solar went*. Its cost shows up in the evening: `GRID → HEAT PUMP 1.0` and `BATTERY → HEAT PUMP 1.2` are two rows for one appliance, so a busy house gets long.

**C2 · By consumer** — one row per thing drawing power, longest bar = biggest draw, and the bar is segmented by source. The evening row reads `HEAT PUMP · grid + battery · 2.2 kW` with a two-colour bar. Row count is constant no matter how the flows split. This is the one I'd ship.

**C3 · In / out** — two columns that always add to the same number; the balance *is* the reading. Most instrument-like and the most compact, but it never says which source fed which load.

Two decisions worth your eye:

- **The wallbox and the car are two things.** The wallbox is a meter (kW), the car is a battery (%). Same split as your grid meter vs the home battery — and it's why the car still reads `78% · plugged in` while drawing nothing.

Installed. A stopped flow now leaves in three beats rather than blinking out:

| beat | duration | what happens |
|---|---|---|
| rest | 10 s | row stays put, reading `0 W` |

The pause is the point — you see the row *read zero* instead of it simply not being there. And the collapse is deliberately separate from the fade: doing both at once would still shift everything below while you're looking at it. A flow that comes back before the fade finishes just picks up where it was.

Row order is sticky for the same reason: a row never moves once placed, and new transfers join at the end, so nothing jumps under your finger. The 500 ms repaint ticker only runs while something is actually leaving.

Base directory for this skill: /tmp/claude-1001/bundled-skills/2.1.237/9c9e45a2731f7f411cb05f07a82ad8ba/dataviz

# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values — touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe — run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure — do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job — magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). → `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) — each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. → `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette — run the script, don't reason about ΔE.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,…>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory — or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   the normal-vision floor, and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, ≥8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. → `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer — by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. → `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For ≥ 2 series a legend is always present and ≤ 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box — the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** — its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout — open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** — it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue — it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale → two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake — see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light→dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD ΔE ≥ 8 is the
  target (OKLab ×100); 6–8 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A
  normal-vision floor below 15 is a hard FAIL — full-color readers can't tell the
  pair apart; re-step it on the adjacent pairlist (secondary encoding does not excuse
  this one); under `--pairs all` cut series or facet instead — see check 4. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view — it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for ≥ 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** — values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance — every value filled in — is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical — steps distinct from categorical |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

## Reference files

| File | What it answers |
|------|-----------------|
| `references/choosing-a-form.md` | Which chart type / is it even a chart? |
| `references/color-formula.md` | The four jobs, the six checks, snap-to-passing |
| `references/marks-and-anatomy.md` | Mark specs, spacers, labels, figures, hero number |
| `references/interaction.md` | Tooltips & hover, filters & time ranges |
| `references/components.md` | The pieces a chart is made of — build each in plain HTML |
| `references/anti-patterns.md` | **What goes wrong — check every chart against this** |
| `references/palette.md` | **The reference palette instance** — every parameter, filled in; swap for your brand's |
| `scripts/validate_palette.js` | Runnable six-checks validator (run it; don't eyeball) |
